content: Blepharokeratoconjunctivitis (BKC) is an inflammatory condition that affects the surface of the eye and the eyelids. It can occur in both children and adults. This condition involves structural changes in the eyelids, dysfunction of the meibomian glands, and inflammation of the conjunctiva and cornea. Chronic inflammation of the cornea can result in complications such as scarring, vascularization, and corneal opacity. In children, BKC can cause significant symptoms, including eye irritation, excessive tearing, sensitivity to light (photophobia), and even vision loss. Vision loss in pediatric BKC patients may arise from corneal opacity, refractive errors, or amblyopia (lazy eye). Treatment for BKC is aimed at addressing the obstruction of the meibomian gland openings, managing the bacterial flora on the eyelid margins and conjunctiva, and reducing ocular surface inflammation. Dietary modifications, such as increasing the intake of essential fatty acids (EFAs), may also provide therapeutic benefits. Both topical and systemic treatments are utilized in managing BKC, but this review specifically focuses on systemic treatments. The objective of this review was to evaluate and compare the efficacy and safety of systemic treatments, including antibiotics, nutritional supplements, and immunosuppressants, either as standalone therapies or in combination, for children aged 0 to 16 years with BKC. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, the ISRCTN registry, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The search spanned from January 1946 to April 2016, and no restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of the studies. The last search was performed on April 21, 2016. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving systemic treatments in children aged 0 to 16 years with a clinical diagnosis of BKC. The review planned to include studies comparing a single systemic medication to a placebo, as well as studies comparing two or more active treatments. Studies in which participants received additional therapies, such as topical antibiotics, anti-inflammatory agents, lubricants, warm lid compresses, and lid margin cleaning, were also eligible for inclusion. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, categorizing studies as 'definitely include,' 'definitely exclude,' or 'possibly include.' For studies in the 'possibly include' category, the full text was reviewed to make a final decision regarding inclusion or exclusion. Unfortunately, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this Cochrane review. No randomized controlled trials have been conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of systemic treatments for BKC in children. Additionally, there is a lack of standardized outcome measures for this condition. The authors concluded that there is currently no clinical trial evidence to support the use of systemic treatments for BKC in children. Future trials are necessary to assess the efficacy and safety of both existing and novel treatments. Furthermore, the development of standardized outcome measures is essential to capture both objective clinical findings and patient-reported outcomes related to the condition and its treatments.
